lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Recently I was reading through the book, uh, a Steinbach history book of all things, Reflections of Our Heritage, that was printed in 1971 by Dirksen Printers, and it was— Abe Warkentin had a lot of input, among others, into that book. And it's a collection of stories from our beginnings. There's a chapter on administration, and it tells many stories of different issues the community leadership had to deal with before incorporation in 1946. So here's just a few stories. From 1874 up until 1946, Steinbach was a village district under the direction of the Arm of Hanover. And it was at that time the Arm of Hanover even built their council chambers in Steinbach. They were in council chambers, I think, until 2010. It wasn't until 1912 that the village of Steinbach was properly surveyed. Dividing it into lots and blocks and all the other land divided among the owners. In all, 22 quarter sections of land were brought under the new system. It took 3 years of managing with the different landowners and coming to different meetings to get an agreement, as the majority of the original lot lines had all changed. In 1920, Steinbach became an unincorporated village district within the RM of Hanover. And a 3-man committee was established to look after the management of the new village. The very first meeting took 1 hour and they appointed J.J. Reimer secretary and they hired him with an annual salary of $35. Troy. Opened a bank account at the bank— at the Royal Bank. That means we've been dealing with the Royal Bank for well over 100 years and directed the new secretary to buy the necessary books and stamps. The committee held regular ratepayer meetings for anyone wishing to attend and took an interest in community affairs. These ratepayer meetings were open with final decisions left to the 3-person committee. Often the contentious issues, the ratepayers also got to vote. At one ratepayer meeting, it was decided to appoint a constable at a salary of $30 per month until December 31st, 1920. So he had 6 months of work.

Fire protection was very important, and 2 chemical fire engines were purchased and placed at J.R. Friesen Garage, which is today Fairway Ford, and the K.R. Barkman property, where— close to where the fire hall sits today.

Some expenditures were $292 to dig 3 community wells. Chemical tanks for the fire pumps were $998, and stationary postage for the whole year was $12.75. Other interesting notes of council is setting community business hours. It was passed and they set those hours, the 6-day-per-week hours and what the businesses could be open. And they also passed a bylaw forbidding obscene language on the streets. I don't know how they enforced it. And the need to build suitable accommodations for those persons that were arrested. In July of 1921, the ratepayers of Steinbach voted 39 to 11 in favour of installing 15 electric lights on Main Street And they were to be installed in a zigzag fashion. This was a case where the ratepayers actually got to vote at a council meeting, or at a committee meeting. On December 30th, 1921 meeting, a resolution passed that stated, whereas P.T. Barkman and Sons build a flour mill in Steinbach, and whereas in our opinion such a flour mill would be of a great service to Steinbach and the arm of Hanover, exempting the said Flour mill from all municipal taxation for a period of 10 years. It was precedent-setting. At the December 15th, 1923 meeting, a major controversy arose after the meeting when the community heard that the 3-man committee had passed a motion to buy a village queen for $1,500 with no accompanying information. When there was a large contingent at the next meeting, Of ratepayers. It was brought to the attention of the ratepayers that the explanation for it was it was a power-driven fire pump that was purchased. But that's an odd name for a fire pump. In 1932, decisions were made to switch off the streetlights and reduce village staff and staff wages due to shortage of funds. This is during the Dirty '30s. Lights were turned back on in February, 6 months later in 1933. But it took another 2 years for staff salaries to be reinstated to the previous levels. In 1943, at the July meeting, it was decided that the cow herdsman be directed to stop blowing his horn on the streets of Steinbach and that Constable Sobring confiscate the horn if the practice continued. For those of you that don't know what a cow herdsman is, I don't think there's any here old enough to remember that, the cow herdsman would start at one end of the village and he would blow his horn and the cows would be released from the barns and he would herd them down Steinbach's Main Street to the, to the community pastor where he would take care of them all day. And then for the evening milking, he'd have them all back to the barns, but he would blow his horn. And I guess it was annoying for some people who needed to sleep in. In 1944, a committee was formed to begin looking at the incorporation for Steinbach as a village, and that took place officially in 1946. This represents but a few of the decisions council of 100-plus years ago had to contend with. It would be interesting to know if some of these are still on the books. While we have moved way beyond what those councils would have envisioned for Steinbach, some of the early decisions moved our community to where we are today. To that end, it would be interesting to know how the decisions we make today might be reported at some future council meeting opening 100 years from now. Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.text: Why is infill housing important to Steinbach? Housing for all. And this will also provide an optimum location for those employed at Bethesda. I think that's a very important note. Financial sustainability. Infill is all about options in a neighbourhood and creating homes and spaces that fit diverse financial needs. Good infill development can lead to increased use of local amenities and allow city services to reach more residents at a lower cost. Building in existing neighborhoods helps save taxpayers money because additional roads, sewers, services, and infrastructure associated with building out are avoided. By densifying, we create walkable neighborhoods that reduce a resident's reliance on cars Which has a direct effect on their monthly expenses. Neighbours of infill homes can benefit financially as new and diverse housing becomes available. When new infill replaces older homes with low assessed values, this can have a positive impact on the overall value of the neighbourhood. Infill housing provides attractive housing for many who wouldn't otherwise be able to enjoy and contribute to the neighbourhood. Keeping neighbourhoods alive. Neighbourhoods are living organisms. They grow, change, and evolve over time. Many homes in mature neighbourhoods are already at or nearing the end of their life cycle. Infill housing provides the next lease on life for these properties. Infill can also revitalize the social well-being of the area by bringing more families and diverse compositions into existing neighbourhoods. This in turn contributes to efficient utilization of schools and public amenities. By gradually increasing the number of people in the area, Local businesses prosper and economic activity increases. Multigenerational living. Infill housing creates flexibility spanning generations. Infill housing makes room for diverse family structures by creating spaces for parents, children, grandparents, and renters to coexist in the same community. Many of our older neighborhoods have housing stock built in the 1940s, the '50s, and the '60s, mostly on large lots. These homes and neighbourhoods need renewal, and while change is hard, it is essential to the health of our community. This proposed location on Home Street, close to Hospital Street, is well suited for this use, especially because it's so close to downtown. It's a perfect walkable location within minutes of 2 elementary schools, restaurants, grocery stores, banks, a credit union, butcher shop, our library, and what will be an amazing event centre. It's also just 120 metres, or about 2 minutes, away from a growing major local employer, Bethesda Hospital. Walkable neighbourhoods are good for our city. People want to be close to services, shopping, and work. For trips under 10 minutes, many people will consider walking. A comprehensive study by the consulting firm Arup found that pedestrians support local business, help to realize safer streets, and make for a more sociable city. People who walk are in better health, experience mental health improvements, and are far more likely to care for the places in which they walk. Our downtown businesses are locally owned and they keep money circulating within our economy, within the community. Adding 40 to 60 residents within easy walking distance means more clients, revenue, and economic goodness for our downtown. A few objectors suggest that multifamily apartments should be built somewhere else, which often means out on the sprawling edges of town, closer to the big box stores that send their revenues out of our city. I wonder how many signatures one would get if downtown business owners and their employees were asked about this zoning change request. Newcomers to a neighbourhood are not a threat. They're just like you and me. They don't want noise. They have their own parking spots. They appreciate privacy, and they also get upset by reckless drivers. Many of the objections we heard tonight are from fear. They're also suppositions not borne out by facts. The people who will eventually live here want what you want— safe streets and good neighbours.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 6
lines.label: Resident 6
lines.text: And please know that builders and developers, their livelihood, it requires them to be open to finding win-win solutions. Privacy, lighting, parking, noise, traffic— there are ways to address these and to lessen their impacts. All it takes are conversations. One thing is certain: our city will continue to grow. How it grows will affect us all. Infill development, better land use, and residential renewal is the way forward to a more prosperous city that works for everyone. Please consider the best interests of our whole city and support this zoning change request. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 7
lines.label: Resident 7
lines.text: Thank you, Council, ladies and gentlemen. My name is [Resident 7]

lines.speaker: Resident 7
lines.label: Resident 7 [medium]
lines.text: [Resident 7]

lines.speaker: Resident 7
lines.label: Resident 7
lines.text: And Luke is my son. I have to say that I was very, very thrilled when I moved back to the Steinbach area. I was gone to Saskatchewan for 15 years, and I was thrilled when I came back. And I know I did come back to visit, but, you know, it's not the same as when you move and you settle back in. to see a lot of the things that have happened here while I was gone. And I would like to commend the existing administration as well as the previous administrations for having a vision of keeping the downtown part of Steinbach alive. And it's evidenced in a number of things that I see when I came back, you know, like the new credit union. And now, of course, this new event centre is phenomenal, following the lead of a place like Winnipeg did with their hockey rink. Do stuff close to the people instead of like people having to, you know, go a long way to do anything. And a lot of the places, I'm amazed at how many of the small businesses have survived. And compared to what I saw in the last years of my trucking career, I traveled from Saskatchewan down to the Mexico border and mostly serviced rural customers.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 7
lines.label: Resident 7
lines.text: Which means that I drove through a lot of smaller cities. And it was amazing to see and talk to local people how the downtowns were just like crumbling and falling down, boarded up, houses empty, businesses closed. And I could name you city after city, especially the range from 10,000 to 25,000 people.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 7
lines.label: Resident 7
lines.text: That the city has grown, but the downtown is dead. The downtown is gone. One gas station in a 20,000 population city in downtown. You have to drive like 10 miles to get gas. And the things that we can do in downtown Steinbach with the hairdressers that, like a lot of the businesses have been mentioned already in the presentations previous, But there's so many others that weren't mentioned that are also close and accessible to this. So we need to keep people living near the downtown if those businesses are gonna thrive and— I should say survive, but thrive. That's what everybody hopes for, right? So I really think in the big picture of things, just like the gentleman who preceded me is that looking at the whole picture, it's understandable that there are some people, their life will change. And I think all of you who are here and are part of this administration have seen a lot of change. And I'll never forget when I first came to Steinbach and I got to know the businessman that was my employer personally, we got a great relationship. Mr. [name withheld], and he said to me one day in his office, and this goes back to about 1980, he said, you know, [Resident 7], he says, if we're not going forward, we're going backward. 25 years later, when I was a top-level executive for a company in Winnipeg that had 1,000 employees, the owner of that company, we met weekly in his office, and he says, you know, to me, [Resident 7], If we're not going forward, if we're not growing, we're going backward. And I think the City of Steinbach has adopted that and done a great job and is doing a great job of making sure that we have growth. But we need growth downtown as well as around the edges.

lines.speaker: Resident 7
lines.label: Resident 7 [medium]
lines.text: Thank you kindly.

lines.speaker: Resident 8
lines.label: Resident 8
lines.text: My name is [Resident 8]. I live at 401 Walnut Street, and I quite frequently walk down to Main Street, which is a farther distance away from Main Street than Hospital Street. It's not impossible to walk. That's what the sidewalks are there for. But I would like to address the issue of affordability that was brought up here, where people talk about cheap housing, the fact that we have, you know, 0% vacancies. People who are trying to move here, seeing this as a desirable city. If we don't allow for infill housing and we force these potential mixed-use density zones to be on the outskirts of town, It will keep property values lower and technically more affordable, but it ignores taxation. When you push something farther away on the outskirts of town or not next to the current existing development with mixed uses between low density and medium density, that means you have to expand the road out into town. You have to take away potential farmland.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Resident 8
lines.label: Resident 8
lines.text: You have to bulldoze existing trees on the outskirts of town. You have to expand the water infrastructure so that you can build pipes out to these new developments that are put somewhere else. You have to expand the electrical grid. You have to expand the sewage maintenance. You have to expand sidewalks. These things are not a one-time payment. They cost money to maintain over time. If you don't allow for infill inside of the city, You will raise your effective tax rate, and by forcing these people to live in single-family dwellings instead of in mixed residential uses, you bring fewer people into the city at a time. Which means while at the same time increasing your tax burden, you have fewer people in the city you are sharing that increased burden amongst. If you were to split a bill, would you rather split it with 1 person or 10 people? One of them is going to be Effectively cheaper, and everyone understands that. By keeping the property values low, you do make it theoretically more affordable to move here, but you also drastically increase your tax rate over the long term. Like, these roads need maintenance. People know that their tax dollars go to maintain roads, and if you don't build on existing infrastructure, that means you will necessarily have to expand and build new infrastructure that increases the burden of this council's budget. So I would just like to point out the fact that there are many existing cities in the world where we can see that population density does not necessarily correlate to all these negative impacts. For example, Tokyo, Japan has a population density 13 times higher than that of Steinbach, And it's consistently rated one of the safest places in the world to live. In addition to that, if you think about going on vacation to places like Europe in terms of traffic, if you go to an old European city that was built with these ideas of density in mind, even in the urban areas, there is actually a decrease in traffic because when more people live closer together, you increase walkability and potential access to public transportation. Which means in the long term, fewer cars will be on the road, not more. It was only after World War II that we started building our suburbs this way and increased our demand of traffic. But if you look throughout all of history and the places you like to vacation to that are older and have been around longer, they understood the prospect of building for the long term. And I would just like to urge all of you to consider how many of you personally know someone right now who cannot afford to buy a home and the fact that we are in a housing crisis. And then think about the idea that we're going to, you know, deny potential development of, you know, mixed-use residential housing over concerns that can very easily and have been addressed And not just other parts of the world, but within our own country.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 9
lines.label: Resident 9
lines.text: So my name is [Resident 9], and I live at 276 Hanover Street. Our house is immediately across the street from the homes that would be immediately impacted by these properties.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 9
lines.label: Resident 9
lines.text: I'm here to stand in solidarity and support with the neighbors that are coming to speak out against this property. I have lived in this same block for the last 22 years, and we have chosen to live in this block specifically for the reason that it is single-family homes with larger lots and mature trees. This is one of the charming things about living on Hanover. And when you look out on the street and see all the trees hanging over the street and the magic of living in such a beautiful neighborhood, we are choosing to live there. We hope to retire and stay in our same home and enjoy the beauty of living in a neighborhood that has so many lovely homes with lovely neighbors. And I feel that a neighborhood changing with a 3-story apartment with all of these families living together Thank you. I think that the proposed development would drastically change not only the appearance of the neighborhood, but increase a lot of the traffic. I also want to speak to what the developer was saying about their hope for the building would increase the diversity of the ages of people that would be living in the neighborhood. And I think if the council members would just take a moment and look out into the foyer outside, you would see a large number of people that really care about their neighborhood Thank you. And it's a community of diverse ages as well. It's not just old seniors living on these streets. It's a lot of young families. And I can attest personally living on our street to the homes that were immediately across from us and next to us used to be R2 rentals or a rental across the street, and they have been purchased by families who are renovating, investing their own funds in improving Their property value by making an affordable home a more beautiful home that their family can enjoy, that has a yard, that has mature trees, and it has improved over the last 5 years. It's remarkable how many homes the homeowners are taking that time and using their funds, which are limited for a lot of families, but they are investing it into their property and beautification of their property. And I just would hate to see that change. Now for our home, We are not directly impacted by the view of a 3-storey apartment, but I am concerned for the people who live immediately across the street from us who will lose all privacy in their backyard. Yes, there's a hedge in the front, but they are going to lose all those— those homes are now going to have 3 storeys of people looking down on their yards. And I wonder If we were all honest here, how many of us would like to have that invasion of privacy of 3 stories of homes with people with balconies on their deck looking down into your yard when you're having your family time or privacy where you just want to have date night or whatever it might be, to have all of that audience there on your yard? That is a huge concern for me. So I am concerned on behalf of those people that will be directly impacted. And I want to stand with support of those neighbours that are against this proposition. So thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 10
lines.label: Resident 10
lines.text: My name is [Resident 10]. I live at 388 Hospital Street. I submitted a letter to the city councillors on Friday with a petition with about 43 signatures, as mentioned before. I wasn't planning to speak, but with all the things that have come up, I thought that it would be a good opportunity. So since we're talking about Tokyo and Europe, I'll talk about northwestern Ontario where I grew up. I grew up in low-income housing. I'm breaking a cycle of poverty and renting in my family line. I live at Hospital Street now for 15 years with my husband, [Resident 12], and my 3 boys. We have had all our babies at Bethesda. It's been great to just walk across the street when you're in labor and give birth. All this to say, like, I'm very content with my home. Like, we've been looking around in the past number of years to see if there's anywhere else we'd possibly like to move in Steinbach area. And the affordability is just there with this area. I just feel like it should stay single-family homes. I met like so many neighbors going around with the petitions that are just having like their first baby. There's a couple of homeschooling moms with boys that are, you know, they want to stay home and homeschool. I work myself part-time, so I feel like if we get rid of these homes, it's just bumping families out of their neighborhood and they're like, where are the options? So I feel like switching this neighborhood out and adding an apartment when we have space, like we have space to build, this is Canada, like there is land. I just feel like it could be built somewhere else and the neighborhood should stay as is. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Is there anyone? Okay, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Resident 11
lines.label: Resident 11
lines.text: Hi, my name is [Resident 11]. I live at 398 Hospital Street. Me and my husband purchased our home 10 years ago because of the neighborhood. We knew that we needed a first home. We wanted something with a big yard that our children could grow up in.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 11
lines.label: Resident 11
lines.text: We wanted a community that we knew our children could make friends with, that we'd have multiple families that could look out for our children as well as us look out for theirs. We recently had new neighbors in our backyard a couple years ago. We have some new neighbors beside us. We get along great with them. We enjoy them. We talk to them when we're outside.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 11
lines.label: Resident 11
lines.text: Winter's a little harder, you know, it's kind of cold, but the community that's in this area, the atmosphere, just the fact that everybody kind of looks out for everybody else has been really enjoyable, and it makes me want to stay in this area. We, like previous people have said, they've looked at other areas, and yes, I would love to upgrade to a bigger home, but Thank you. I love the neighborhood and I would rather stay in this neighborhood the way it is with single-family homes, with families looking out for each other, than to have a 3-story complex move in, especially on a street that already has so much trouble with traffic and parking. With us live— with me living on Hospital Street and the parking being removed, the street parking, Thank you. I'll admit it's been nice for us, but at the same time, we've seen how it's impacted the streets around us. Home Street, there is always parking all the way down, people parked on the street. If we want visitors to come over, they have to sometimes park 3 or 4 streets away because we've been taking away parking around the hospital, which is a good thing, I agree. But to add now a 3-story complex with the extra parking that's going to come from people visiting those people in the complex, Not just the people living there, I think will sorely impact parking in the area. The building alone will impact the atmosphere of the neighborhood, and all in all, it's just not a good fit for this neighborhood. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 12
lines.label: Resident 12
lines.text: Hello, my name is [Resident 12]. I'm at 388 Hospital Street. Thanks for giving me an opportunity to speak. I just want to reiterate some of the things that my wife already mentioned and [Resident 1] already said about just kind of zooming in on the bigger picture here, or zooming out a little bit. What our big concern is, is Essentially the removal of affordable entry-level homes from, from our neighborhood. I just feel like taking away more single-family homes is just adding another blow to the aspirations of first-time buyers in our city. Steinbach prides itself on being a place where families can put down roots and invest in their future. By demolishing homes such as these to put up rental units, we are narrowing the path to to homeownership for young families. As was mentioned, the neighborhood already has— there's many families that are having their first child or raising school-aged children, and these older neighborhoods are desirable for families of this type. And the disappearance of homes such as this from the market, replaced by rental properties, threatens to erode this much-loved aspect of our community. Homeownership is not just a transaction, it's the cornerstone of a vibrant and resilient community. It provides residents with a stake in the future, a sense of belonging, and foundation for financial security. While we acknowledge the need for rental properties and Kingdom Home Building has a vision for excellence in rentals, we believe that they should not come at the expense of an established neighborhood such as ours. Thank you for your time.

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor

lines.text: Good evening.

lines.speaker: Resident 13
lines.label: Resident 13
lines.text: My name is [Resident 13] and I'm at 271 Hanover Street. I've been there for almost 5 years. Also a university student and a mother, and this is a very precious time that I'm taking out of my evening to be here and oppose this. In terms of communication, despite being directly adjacent to the rear of the proposed property, I never received any communication whatsoever from the developer about this property and about what was going to happen. My backyard is right there. There would be a property right up against it. During the construction of the event centre and the hospital, our street and our area has put up with a lot. During the pile— while the piles were were being driven for the event centre. I actually had things fall off of my walls. I was woken up in the morning multiple times by very loud pile driving and construction noises. There is mud on our street constantly. There is cars absolutely packing our roads constantly, both on Home Street and on my street, Hanover. And our neighbourhood has put up with a lot. And I think a lot of us were really looking forward to the construction Thank you. So I would like to see any construction taking a pause after these projects were complete. In terms of affordable housing, I am a homeowner today because of this neighbourhood. And I would not be a homeowner if this neighbourhood had not been there because it is one of the very, very few affordable housing locations in this city. Even those affordable housing places like Lexington, as someone else mentioned, are Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 13
lines.label: Resident 13 [medium]
lines.text: More expensive.

lines.speaker: Resident 13
lines.label: Resident 13
lines.text: I also, when we initially bought this house, my husband and I considered maybe we would flip it. Maybe we would do some work on it and make a bit of a profit and move somewhere else. It took us very little time being in this neighbourhood to realize this is not a flipping neighbourhood. It is not the type of neighbourhood you put money into a house and you leave. When we moved in, as [Resident 9] mentioned, Thank you. There was a lot of rental properties. Our home was previously a rental property and it was quite run down. It was old. We put some work into it and over the next couple of years, the properties around us also were purchased and had very amazing families put hard-earned money into these houses to make them forever homes. And this is not a— in a house that we plan on flipping and Selling for profit. This is a home for us, and this has become a home for all of the, the neighbors around us as well who have done similar things to their properties. We've put our heart and soul into this place. We bought it because it was older, affordable, mature trees, large lots. Like [Resident 9] said, our neighborhood has all kinds of people. My neighbor to one side is a senior. My neighbor in another area are expecting their first child. There's middle-aged people, there's all kinds of people. There's lots of diversity. And all of us in this neighbourhood consider Steinbach and this specific area to be a very cozy home for us. And it is not— you can build your development somewhere else. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 14
lines.label: Resident 14
lines.text: Good evening. My name is [Resident 14]. I live at 36 Giesbrecht Street. I am in the unique position to comment on this building development because I live next to a bunch of homes and apartments built by Kingdom Homes on First Street, one street down from me.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 14
lines.label: Resident 14
lines.text: I believe this notion that this area is affordable, it's no longer affordable. After COVID, That kind of ruined things. I am looking to buy a house, but I don't really think that's possible in the future. So renting is my only opportunity, and this just increases the opportunities for that. As he said, there is no vacancy in buildings like these, and there's always applicants. So that limits my options there as well. And I would like to comment on the fact that people seem to think that the building won't fit into this neighborhood. I believe it'll fit perfectly into this neighborhood. You have multiple large buildings like the hospital there and the arena about one block over, and those are big towering buildings talking like 40, 50, 60 feet tall. And then you compare that to literally just across the street.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Resident 14
lines.label: Resident 14
lines.text: 50 feet from it is a small one-story home. It doesn't make much sense, but if you build a 3-story building there and transition, kind of like a step-down idea, it provides a transition and a buffer to the neighborhood and allows that area to be kind of— I don't know how to say it— kind of smoothed over and transitioned with the rest of the buildings around it. That's about all I have to say. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Is there anyone else with comments, questions, or objections to this file? Okay.

lines.speaker: Resident 15
lines.label: Resident 15
lines.text: Good evening. My name is [Resident 15]. I'm at 368 Hospital with Thank you, Madam Mayor.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you, Councillor Lococo.

lines.speaker: Resident 15
lines.label: Resident 15
lines.text: Thank you, Madam Mayor.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you, Councillor Lococo, and thank you, Councillor [Resident 2].

lines.speaker: Resident 15
lines.label: Resident 15
lines.text: I'm going to repeat a few things because everybody made really good points, mostly everybody. I think a lot has been asked of this neighbourhood already with the construction that's been happening. It's not a derelict, boarded-up neighbourhood with a gas station 10 miles away. If it was, maybe it would qualify for infill housing. Nobody's arguing the merits of infill housing, um, but where's the balance? Um, there already is quite a bit in that area and around it, and I know council has challenges that you have money that goes out, you have—

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 15
lines.label: Resident 15
lines.text: You must have money that comes in, and that would serve that purpose. But my concern is, and I'm not trying to be smart-alecky, but if you look 30 years into the future, maybe 40, that entire map will look like the bottom left-hand corner.

lines.speaker: Resident 15

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Resident 15
lines.label: Resident 15

lines.speaker: Resident 8
lines.label: Resident 8
lines.text: I'd like to add one thing. My name's [Resident 8] from 401 Walnut. The reason that the bottom left-hand of this map looks so blighted is because everything that was greenery there had to be bulldozed to build infrastructure such as roads because the growth of the city with every house being an individually owned single-family dwelling unit—

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: [Resident 8].

lines.speaker: Resident 8
lines.label: Resident 8
lines.text: That all of the amenities had to be placed on the outskirts of town because everything had to be spread farther apart. When everything is spread farther apart and you bulldoze to make giant parking lots to accommodate for the cars because everything is farther away, so you can't walk and have to drive there, you necessarily take away more of the natural greenery and nature.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 8
lines.label: Resident 8
lines.text: If you think about a road with 50 people on it, if each of those people is individually in their own car, it will take up much more space than one bus with 50 people on it on the same road, even though it's the same number of people. Density means that things can be closer together and not as spread far apart. When you spread things farther apart, That is what causes people to have to drive to go places. The reason there are concerns about traffic is because we have a lack of infill. The farther away you push something from your own backyard, the more you necessitate car use, the more you have to bulldoze for parking lots, and the more expensive it becomes in the long term to maintain it.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thanks.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.text: Good evening.

lines.speaker: Resident 16
lines.label: Resident 16
lines.text: My name is [Resident 16]. I live at 251 Home Street. Thank you for inviting us to be here, to participate, and to hear from us as the neighbors of Home Street. I'd just like to read the email that I had sent earlier and again, just formally state my opposition to this matter. It was also mentioned that there's 43 people that have currently signed the petition. And while we all here can, can speak to the matter, we can say various opinions, ultimately the decision is yours. And I'd just humbly like to ask, how much opposition does it take to be heard on this matter?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 16
lines.label: Resident 16
lines.text: So I'll just proceed with my, my email. Good morning. I want to state my opposition to the rezoning of Home Street to make a multifamily building and parkade. We live on Home Street near the 274 and 268 Home Street addresses. This proposal would be extremely upsetting and disruptive to our family and the current residents residing in the area. The Home Street area is an advantageous neighborhood for families presently, as it offers a quaint, mature neighborhood close to the amenities of the downtown area. However, rezoning Home Street to add a 3-story, 32-unit multifamily building and parkade will impede these benefits and have a negative impact to the area. Constructing a multifamily building and parkade raises concerns with the substantial increase to traffic Thank you. The proposed development would add significant traffic to the neighborhood, limited parking, demolishing mature trees, light pollution, noise pollution, invading neighbors' privacy, disruption to our homes as the foundations are impacted, and disrupting our homey community. Moreover, the proposal would increase safety concerns by having a significant increase of residents and their co-patriots. It raises concerns from a traffic perspective at an already busy intersection with a heavy flow of traffic on Hospital and Home Street. Vehicles come off Hospital Street onto Home Street quickly and with reduced visibility as it is an angled street and not perpendicular to Hospital. This already causes concerns about safety to a neighborhood filled with young families But, but to add an increase in traffic from a 32-unit multiplex would only exacerbate the problem. We implore you to keep Home Street zoned residential low density and oppose the proposal. Thank you sincerely for your time and consideration.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Okay, I will ask this question one, one last time. Is there anyone here with comments, questions, or objections? Okay, seeing none, I will trust that everyone that's wanted to speak will, will have been able to speak today.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: I'm going to ask— I'm going to ask the developer if you want to address any of the objections.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: No?

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay. Well then, gathering all this information, I will close the public hearing, open the council meeting. Council, how would you like to proceed? Move to close. Councillor Susan Penner.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Is there a seconder?

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: I'll second it.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor) [medium]
lines.text: Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: This is a very difficult file, obviously, given the emotion and the comments we have heard tonight. First of all, I just want to say I can totally understand the construction fatigue in the area, whether it's with all the things going on at the hospital, with the event centre. There's been a lot going on there, and I can, I can definitely understand and empathize that that must be quite taxing. This is my 4th year on council, and since my first term, this council has consistently and intentionally talked about how we keep our downtown healthy and vibrant. There's a lot of research that shows that a healthy downtown is essential to the health of an entire community. We have stuck out our necks before on this. I would say we— when it comes to having the SCU downtown, a lot of effort went into having the SCU build downtown versus is, um, on the outskirts on the north side because we wanted to have our downtown vibrant. When it came to the event center, we took a lot of heat. Um, the majority of people we talked to and during this process wanted to see this event center at a greenfield location outside of town, which exactly would mean that people would need to drive there. It wouldn't be walkable. The cost of Yes. And the cost of servicing would mean the cost of that project would be even higher. So we've really been intentional about making decisions to keep our downtown vibrant. The thing about this project is although it's not in the transition zone, it is very close. And what's interesting, it is right across the street from multi-level development, the hospital, Being right there. It's very close to the event center. I drove by there again and I'm like, today, and I just thought, you know, this is a really good location for a project like this, particularly 'cause it's at the corner of the street. If it wouldn't be at the corner of the street, maybe it'd be given more pause, but the access to it is on that corner really makes it, I think, a good location for a project like that. The other piece I like about it is we're not— we're all aware of the challenges with our healthcare system and finding healthcare workers. If this is a project, because it's right by the hospital, that can, you know, point people in favor of working in our healthcare system in Steinbach, I think even that's just a really big benefit. A couple of other things I really like is that this Thank you. This building has an elevator, and that is very rare in 3-story buildings in our community. Because there's an elevator, that means it gives seniors opportunity to live there because they will not have to do stairs. And we all know our population is aging, so I think that's a real benefit. Or, you know, people who have disabilities as well. This opens us up for an opportunity for them to be in a place that has an elevator. And so I think that's a big benefit as well. We have received opposition for multifamily infill developments before. There's one across from Woodlawn School. There's one kind of behind the library. There's also one that predates my time, but there's a 3-story one there right where the event center is, Maplewood. And I also know Maplewood Manor is actually on Okay. Home Street, and that would be multifamily as well. I really want to empathize. I know change is hard in a neighborhood, and we see it with infill, or we see it in areas where there's been no construction behind a residential area, and all of a sudden a whole new development is going up. Like, so I don't want to— I'm not minimizing, you know, how hard this is maybe for the neighborhood. Having said that, I just I think big picture for the community, for that area, for our downtown, for the hospital, I think the, the benefits outweigh the costs in this particular situation. So for that reason, I'm moving to approve the project.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. The request here is to rezone 2 properties from residential low density to residential medium density. And these, as everybody knows, these are on the corner of Home Street and Reimer Avenue.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Or hospital, I should say.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: And it is—

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: It's in its own transition zone, I would think. It's between the hospital and residential. I really appreciate the comments made and the passion from all the people living in single-family homes in that area. I know that we moved from a single-family home into 50 feet behind our house. When I sit on my deck, 50 feet behind is a 3-storey. I have a 4-storey building and it works very well. There's 9 decks that look onto our backyard and it works. I know that it works. But I'm in favour of this for a number of reasons. The properties are within walking distance of financial institutes, libraries, smaller grocery stores in downtown, recreational activities, and potentially workplace. As mentioned, The hospital's right there. They are going to be employing a lot more people, and this isn't the last expansion, this is just another one. So they will continue to expand. That footprint isn't necessarily today in the right place, but that's where it is, and I'm sure that that footprint is going to continue to expand, meaning more people required to work. That means if we can get— improve our density downtown, improve our— more people living Close by, they will walk to work and they will have those opportunities. Many of our older downtown core are large lot, and we've been struggling with this all over Steinbach, not just in that area. And large lots were very common in Steinbach, in many older communities, parts of the communities, because families— single-family homes were built and with— will hold large gardens and maybe a chicken coop in the backyard. And, but that's what— how they fed their families. And that's no longer what happens today. What happens today, as you all know, those large backyards don't hold gardens or fruit orchards anymore as much. But there are some great trees in Steinbach. I've talked about trees in my openings in the past. But what do we do with these large lots? Developers have told us time over time that to buy a To build a home and rip it down and build another single-family home on these large lots is not feasible. It's not financially feasible to do. So I appreciate the fact that people are fixing up the old homes, but eventually they too will need replacing. But with what if you can't afford a single-family to build, rebuild a single-family home? As indicated in the amenity report, this, the infill policy dictates what actually will be built. So the plan is for a 3-storey. I think the height allowed is 36 feet, if I have that right. But infill policy will dictate exactly what and how it will be built. The last year has not been kind to the people of Home Street and that area. I recognize that because I drive through there on a daily basis. And I also get stopped by the construction and I have to wait for them to back up and I have to listen to their beeping horns. I'm just thankful For all of you that they're not working 24-hour days. And, uh, but I see that too, that there is a frustration that comes with that as well. And our streets will have to be rebuilt. We've stopped— the city has actually planned not to rebuild those streets while that construction is taking place. But expect that once that construction is complete, that there will be street construction or overlay in those areas because of Ongoing.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Ongoing.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: We do need to build our community as— and we've recognized this in our official community plan. Our official community plan started 15 or so years ago, and it lays out how we're— how we expect the city to grow. But we've always talked about growing up instead of out, simply because of the costs in the long term, and we continue to do that. And This makes sense under the future plan and how we've always spoken about higher density in our downtown core and keeping people living in our downtown core. How does— what does that look like? It looks like you grow up, not, not out with, with the urban sprawl, because it is a lot more expensive. Urban sprawl is a lot more expensive in the short term and in the long term for our communities. For me, Moving these lots to medium density, it works. New or current employees of Bethesda or the event centre would— this would give an opportunity to work within our downtown core. There's many jobs in our downtown core, and people could choose to live there, and then they wouldn't need to drive anywhere. I think overall, in our big picture official community plan, I think this works, and for those reasons, I'm in favour of this.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Go ahead, Councillor Zwaagstra.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Well, we're going to have a split vote on this because I'm going to vote against this. And there are a number of reasons why I'm going to— why I'm going to vote against. The point of a public hearing is to hear both from the applicant and also to hear from the neighbourhood. There's a reason why we send out notices to the neighbourhood, because we want to hear feedback from the neighbourhood and we take that into consideration. In this case here, we've heard some very strong feedback from the neighbourhood. And I want to point something out here because, again, anyone can speak during a public hearing, but the people we're really interested in hearing from are the people who actually live in the area. So it's all well and good when we have a few people that come and live far away and want to give their 2 cents and give us sort of a, you know, sort of bit of a lecture about what the neighbourhood should be feeling, but I'm not interested in hearing about Tokyo and their density and all that. I want to hear from the neighbours and I want to hear from the applicant, and that's what I want to focus on. And so in regards to the application here, I think the neighbourhood has made some good points as far as this is not a rundown area. This is a well-established area. It's not in the transitional zone. Yes, it's reasonably close to the transitional zone, but it is not. And the people in this area would like for it to continue as single-family homes.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: There seems to be this assumption that— I understand the reasoning in terms of that, yes, density in general, in theory, is good. But so are single-family homes. Those are good too. I like single-family homes. I live in one. I intend to continue living in a single-family home as long as I can. I do not want to send the message that single-family homes aren't good and that— I'm not seeing anything here that's wrong with single-family homes.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: With how the neighborhood is right now. I'm not hearing any convincing case for what the problem is. Yes, we need more housing, we need more development. We're getting that in Steinbach. That's happening in a variety of areas in the city. But when we have this many people that are coming out that live right there, that are giving some pretty good reasons for why they're not in favor of the change, I think we need to take that into consideration. I also want to point out, as I— when I'd asked the applicant earlier about the question, and I think Members of council, we might be losing sight of this. If this gets approved, we're having another public hearing. We're going to go through this all again because for whatever reason, the applicant did not submit a variance application for the underground parking. Our staff says that the notification was given, and I believe our staff. And so— but we're going to have to go through this all again, and the neighbourhood will all get a chance to comment once again because the applicant The applicant has said that he is for certain going ahead with the underground parking and with this plan that we've had presented to us here. So I don't— I have concerns about the plan itself. I have concerns about just this assumption that we just have to put this change in place. And so, yes, there have been times, many times, when I voted in favour of multifamily developments and rezoning, but in this case, I'm not in favour. I think it's fine leaving it as it is.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Go ahead, Councillor Hiebert.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. This application has put council into an unpopular position, and I'd like to start by thanking the developer for a very good presentation. I'd also like to thank each person that attended here to voice their opinion and to state what their values are and why they want to maintain those values. Yes, this is a single-family area, but we've heard from residents that moved to Steinbach because this is what they wanted. They wanted single-family dwellings. They wanted dwellings that were affordable, and they chose this area. Yes, this area is close to amenities. That's why they chose this area. We hear about 3-storey buildings and density and how people can walk to different amenities. Well, I also see people in this area pushing baby carriages and going downtown.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: These people will be close to the event centre. These people living here in single-family dwellings are close to the hospital. They value the same things that people value in apartment blocks. But these people specifically chose, and they've invested. We've heard of people that have been here for a couple of years, that have been here for 2 years.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: And that have bought buildings that they thought they were going to live in, in a peaceful area for a number of years. And they now see this as not being practical for them in the future, should such a building be built in their area. Yes, maybe it'd be more suitable if there was a duplex or a fourplex For transitioning into this area, but as Deputy Mayor Zwaagstra said, this is not in the transitional zone. This is on the outskirts of it. But in this situation, if that was me, and I know that I shouldn't always make a decision if that was me or if that was my children living there, But I've heard people that are torn living in this area and wanting to stay. So I appreciate every person that came here today and gave their story. And what's important, what are their values? And I've heard you loud and clear.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Anything further, council? Councillor Panter.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor, and I want to thank, uh, the applicant as well as the community that came out, came out today. Um, truth be told, uh, with discussion from both sides and also with there being a split council that has spoken both for and against, I personally don't find much to disagree with on either side of the decision.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: I—

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Pardon me. In terms of a location, I think that this is actually a very good suitable location for medium dense— pardon me—

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: For medium density. It is right downtown.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: It's within walking distance of a lot of the amenities. A lot of the values that I've heard from the community are the same values that individuals that are going into entry-level or renting would hold as well. They want to raise— they want to raise their families.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: They want to—

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: They're younger, they're older. There's a mix. There's a diversity. It's the same for renters as it is for single-family homeowners. I can also appreciate the fact that this is a neighborhood that is well maintained. Generally, when we see infill applications come to us, we see them in more areas that are on the verge of needing redevelopment, areas that have been neglected for for years, sometimes decades, and are in need of redevelopment. So there's a need for it. With regards to looking at the city as a whole, this is a need. We are looking at our official community plan right now in depth, and a 20-year projection is we need to double our population. If we double our population, our population Okay. Outwards, the city will fail. It's just that simple. We cannot double our population sprawling outwards. Having said that, there is also a lot of value of having young families in affordable single-family housing within accessibility to the downtown. It's a nice mix to have that option, especially in a neighbourhood that is being well maintained. So there's benefits to both, but with the neighbours coming out, I will be voting against the motion to approve this development.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor) [medium]
lines.text: Any—

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Go ahead, Councillor Hiebert.

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Mr. Mayor, I want to address— I mean, first of all, I appreciate everybody that's come out and see both sides as well. But I want to address the topic of transport, of traffic. I live on a street, I live on Parkview Crescent, just off of Parkview Crescent on Parkside Place. We have well over 200 apartments at the end of our street and traffic is no impact. There is so little traffic coming out of those 200 suites. And so that part, I would say, is not going to be a big issue, and especially in that area.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: And with the people working probably nearby, I feel this will not impact that. And I think the, the area where this is proposed, I don't have a problem. And it's tough to see change for anybody and everybody here. And I know you don't like what I'm saying, but I will be voting in favor of this.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything in closing?

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: First of all, I'd like to say I actually really like it when we have split votes because I think that's democracy in action. So I think that's really good and I appreciate the comments by my colleagues. Again, regardless of which way this one goes, I do think it is a difficult case and I think we all can see both, both sides of the coin on this one. Yeah, I'll just leave it at that.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Council, this is a difficult decision, and you can ask, you can ask administration. I have been on the phone with them a lot trying to decipher through all the information to make the best decision. And at the end of the day, I do believe because of where it's situated, because the nature of the project, Because of the— it's beside the hospital, all those things. I, I think it's a good fit for the area. And I want to qualify that because I, uh, Councillor Zwaagstra, I do agree with you that we don't want to hear about what's, what's life in Tokyo like. But I get it that there are people that don't live in the area that have experience.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: And I think we need to listen to their experience as well. And I'm going to come from a point of experience now with multifamily. In— I'm going to try and think. It might have been '08. I think it was 2012. We bought a property on Lumber Avenue and there was 2 multifamily behind us, 2 buildings like what Mr. Wiebe wants to build.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: By you guys. There were 2 right behind us. And I would say the exact same things about our neighborhood. We would talk to our neighbors, we would help our neighbors. Um, [name withheld] would— during COVID the neighborhood became so close. Like, every community, I believe every neighborhood in our, in Every neighbourhood in our community has a little micro-community inside of it. And I think that is to be— let me drink— that needs to be celebrated. And you can have that beautiful close community with multifamily in your neighbourhood. It's even— it just multiplies it because there's more people. There wasn't an evening that we weren't outside. That people from the multifamily were walking past our street and they would talk. I remember talking to my wife many times, I'm not doing yard work in the evening when people are walking because I get nothing done. So I would hide in the backyard and I would send her up front to do the yard work in front. But that's how it was. And we just, we loved that community. We loved that neighborhood. It was straight out of necessity that we had to move. My wife's knees were failing, and with a small heritage home, there were lots of steep stairs. So we had to do something. We'd still be there if we could have taken care of that issue. Thank you. But please don't fear multifamily. You can live harmoniously with multifamily and single-family dwellings. It does work. And that microcommunity, I can appreciate it because we loved our people that were beside us. And during one time when our neighbors were having a baby, they had it— it was He was premature. Well, we just— they just— we just said go. We took care of their yard. I snowblowed their yard. Apparently that November, December, it snowed every other day. So I was constantly at their place snowblowing. We took care of them. When our neighbor across the street, she now has passed away, we worked with the family. We helped them, even though we don't live there anymore, we still help them. And, you know, those connections and the connections you're making in your neighbourhood, they're not going to just stay in the neighbourhood. They will last for years and years and years.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor) [medium]
lines.text: And that—

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Because that's how we are. We're people. We're wired for companionship and friendship. So please don't Don't look at, at this as such a negative. There can be a lot of positive to this because we saw the positive of living and we lived with 2 of the same size buildings right behind us. So for that reason, I do believe that, that I think this is a good fit and I will as well vote in favor. And I will also agree with Councillor I do actually like it when we don't have unanimous votes. It shows that council has deliberated and council is thinking hard and serving the community as best we can. Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Thank you. Good job, Susan. Waldo, I guess you're not going to clap for me, eh? You're not going to clap for me.

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: It's going to be that long, too?

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: I know.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Susan, good job.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, council, we'll move on to 6B. This is another public hearing. I think what we'll do is we'll take B and C. Mr. Warkentin, if you could introduce them together and we'll take care of them separately, but we won't do them separately necessarily. Like, so we will introduce them together. So this is for B and C, this conditional use, CU-2024-01. This refers to 330 First Street. And the variance is also the same. It's V-202402. This is also referring to 330 First Street. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Just give me a moment. I've just spilled a cup of water over my notes.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Well, you take a couple minutes to Pick up fiber. Whatever, clean up. I do want to say that the proud new owners of our house on Lumber are sitting right in front of us. Yeah, and we invested significant dollars into it. Okay. That's how transition goes.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Mayor, members of council. As requested, I will introduce both files and then council may proceed to consider both matters. Firstly, application for conditional use, file CU-2024-01, and application for variance, file V-2024-02, both affecting 331st Street in Steinbach.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Owner of the property is Skyprom Marketing Inc. The applicant for the variance and conditional use applications is Waldo Neustader.
